a1: Catherine Susan Genovese was born in Brooklyn on July seventh, nineteen thirty-five, the eldest of five children in an Italian-American family.
Everyone called her Kitty. Friends remembered her as outgoing, quick to laugh, and fiercely independent.
When her family moved to Connecticut, Kitty stayed behind. New York was home.

By nineteen sixty-four, she was managing Ev's Eleventh Hour, a bar in Hollis, Queens. She worked late, she knew the regulars by name, and she was saving her money. She dreamed of one day opening a restaurant of her own.
She shared a small apartment in Kew Gardens with her partner, Mary Ann Zielonko. In nineteen sixty-four, two women could not live openly as a couple. To the neighbors, they were simply roommates.
On the night of March twelfth, Kitty worked until closing. A little after two-thirty in the morning, she locked up, said goodnight, and got into her little red Fiat.
Somewhere along the way home, a man in a white Corvair noticed her car. He followed it all the way to Kew Gardens.
a2: Across Austin Street, a light snapped on. From his window in the Mowbray apartments, Robert Mozer shouted into the dark.
The man ran back to his car and drove away.
Kitty was alive. Badly wounded, she got to her feet and stumbled along the side of the building, toward the back entrance, out of sight of the street.
For a few minutes, Austin Street went quiet again. Lights went out. Some neighbors later said they thought it was a drunk, or a lovers' quarrel.
About ten minutes later, the white Corvair came back.
Moseley searched the parking lot, the train station, the street. He found her in a small vestibule at the back of her building, just a few feet from her own door.
There, he attacked her again. He stabbed her, sexually assaulted her, and took forty-nine dollars from her wallet.
At the top of the stairs, a neighbor named Karl Ross opened his door. He saw what was happening. And he closed it again.
Instead of calling the police, he called a friend for advice. Later, he would explain: I didn't want to get involved.
Sophia Farrar didn't hesitate. She ran out of her apartment and down to the vestibule, not knowing whether the killer was still there. She found Kitty, and held her in her arms.
The police were finally called at about three-fifty in the morning. They arrived within minutes.
Kitty Genovese died in the ambulance on the way to the hospital. She was twenty-eight years old.
a3: Five days later, in Corona, Queens, a resident named Raoul Cleary noticed a stranger carrying a television set out of a neighbor's house, in broad daylight.
The man said he was helping the family move. Cleary didn't believe him. While they talked, another neighbor, Jack Brown, quietly disabled the stranger's car.
When the police arrived, the man was arrested. His name was Winston Moseley.
In custody, Moseley confessed, calmly and in detail, to the murder of Kitty Genovese. And then to two more. Annie Mae Johnson. And Barbara Kralik.
He was twenty-nine years old. A married father, with a steady job and no criminal record. Asked why, he told detectives he had an urge to kill.
a4: Two weeks after the murder, the city editor of The New York Times, A. M. Rosenthal, had lunch with Police Commissioner Michael Murphy. Murphy brought up the Genovese case. One detail, he said, had stayed with him.
On March twenty-seventh, the Times ran the story on its front page.
Thirty-eight respectable, law-abiding citizens, it said, had watched a killer stalk and stab a woman in three separate attacks, over more than half an hour. And not one of them had called the police.
The story exploded. It was read on the radio, preached from pulpits, debated across the country. Kitty Genovese became a symbol of a city where nobody cared.

In nineteen sixty-eight, two psychologists, John Darley and Bibb Latané, set out to test the idea. Students sat alone in small booths, talking over an intercom, when one of them appeared to have a seizure.
When a student believed they were the only one listening, eighty-five percent went for help. When they believed four others could hear it too, only thirty-one percent did.
They called it the bystander effect. The more people who witness an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to act.
a5: But when researchers, journalists and lawyers went back to the evidence, the story began to fall apart.

The first attack happened at three-nineteen in the morning, in March, with most windows shut. Many neighbors heard something. Very few saw anything clearly. Several thought it was a drunk, or a couple fighting.
The second attack, the fatal one, happened inside the vestibule. From the street, and from almost every window, it was invisible.

At least one man shouted from his window, and drove the attacker off. At least one, and possibly two people, called the police after the first attack. And Sophia Farrar went down and held Kitty as she died.
In two thousand seven, psychologists Rachel Manning, Mark Levine and Alan Collins concluded there was no evidence that thirty-eight people had watched and done nothing.
In two thousand sixteen, The New York Times itself acknowledged that its story had grossly exaggerated the number of witnesses, and what they had seen.
Kitty's younger brother, Bill Genovese, spent years tracking down the people who were there that night. His film, The Witness, was released in two thousand fifteen.
a6: In June nineteen sixty-four, Winston Moseley was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. On appeal, his sentence was reduced to life in prison.
In nineteen sixty-eight, during a hospital trip in Buffalo, he overpowered a guard and escaped. He took hostages and assaulted a woman before he was captured again.
He was denied parole eighteen times. He died in prison on March twenty-eighth, two thousand sixteen, at the age of eighty-one. He outlived Kitty by fifty-two years.
The thirty-eight witnesses were, in large part, a myth. But the question the story asked was real, and it has never gone away.
When you hear someone scream in the night, when you're not sure what it is, and you're not sure anyone else will help, what do you do?
